summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised in Vietnam and has not been criminalised in Vietnamese history; the Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The 1812 Gia Long Code, Article 332, criminalised prostitution and illicit sexual activity such as extra-marital sex, and in rare cases prosecutions could be brought against homosexual conduct under those labels, but pre-colonial enforcement was inconsistent enough that little to no state action is recorded.

Article 37 of the 2015 Civil Code recognised transgender people's right to change their legal gender. The amendment was passed by the National Assembly on 24 November 2015 by 282 votes to 84 and took effect in January 2017, allowing people who have undergone sex reassignment to register under their preferred sex; a November 2015 milestone separately allowed people who had changed gender to apply for a change of civil status. Sex reassignment surgery was previously illegal, which forced transgender people to travel to Thailand for the procedure. The implementing bill has never been enacted, so the statutory right has no operative procedure.

Under the Law on Citizen Identification, in force from 1 July 2024, transgender citizens may change their identity card when undergoing gender transition, but must present confirmation documents, and the change's legal effect depends on passage of a Gender Affirmation Law. A draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights was expected to be discussed by the National Assembly with completion targeted for 2020 and never materialised; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of February 2026, and the implementing legislation promised for 2017 is still unimplemented. Obstacles to gender-affirming care and to changing the legal gender marker therefore persist.

No Vietnamese law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, according to Freedom House as cited by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada in June 2022. Amnesty International's 2025 report finds that LGBTI people's rights lack meaningful protection in both law and practice.

Same-sex couples may not be prosecuted: fines on same-sex marriages were abolished by government decree on 24 September 2013, effective 11 November 2013, and same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts. Unions still confer no legal rights or recognition. Conversion therapy has been prohibited since 3 August 2022 under Ministry of Health Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC, which states that homosexuality, bisexuality and being transgender are not illnesses and that LGBTQ+ people may not be forced into treatment.

Public assembly space narrowed in 2025. Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events; the Asia director of Human Rights Watch, Patricia Gossman, described this as a worrying sign of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against Vietnam's long-standing reputation for tolerance in the region. Pride events had previously been held openly, with the first parade in Hanoi on 5 August 2012 and events in around 34 further cities and provinces by 2017.

Transgender visitors should expect document-related friction in healthcare settings. A United Nations feature of 30 November 2024 records transgender women being asked at medical encounters whether they are male or female and why their appearance does not match their identity card, together with heightened scrutiny and an economic- and stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence, concentrated among transgender women in northern provinces and among ethnic minorities. A June 2023 report describes healthcare providers as respectful in person but says administrative red tape undoes that for four transgender Vietnamese whose cases it documents. Outright International's March 2026 overview frames accessible legal recognition as the unresolved barrier to non-discriminatory care.
tangentialFactors:
Amnesty International's Viet Nam 2025 report places the position of LGBTI people inside a wider pattern of repression: vaguely worded Penal Code articles 109, 116, 117 and 331 were used to arrest at least 43 people during 2025, and proposed press-law rules would require disclosure of sources. Viet Nam was re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council for a term running to 2028. The same restrictive climate governs the environment in which Pride permissions are granted or refused.

LGBTIQ organisations operate openly in Vietnam but under government surveillance, according to Outright International's March 2026 overview.

A January 2015 proposal from the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute to the Ministry of Public Security urged that homosexual and transgender prisoners be housed separately from the general prison population to protect them from sexual harassment, citing US California figures that 67% of homosexual and transgender prisoners had suffered harassment and a 2014 survey in which most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. The institute noted that Vietnamese prison infrastructure then allowed transgender prisoners only solitary confinement or mixing with the general population, so no wing matched to a prisoner's gender identity existed, and asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome has been documented.

Before the 2015 Civil Code amendment, surgical transition required travel to a neighbouring jurisdiction. Lighthouse Vietnam's October 2024 study documents the forms that sexual orientation and gender identity change efforts take in the Vietnamese context and sets out data needs, indicating that such practices persist despite the 2022 Ministry of Health dispatch.
localsOnly:
Discrimination against LGBT students is documented at scale. A 2015 study found around 44% of Vietnamese LGBT students aged 14 to 22 faced stigma, discrimination and violence because of their identities; a 2014 USAID report showed 54% of LGBT students said their school was not safe, with many dropping out, and of those who experienced violence one third had thought about suicide and half of those had attempted it. Eighty-five per cent of transgender students said they dropped out because of assault and bullying. A 2015 UNESCO study found 19% of students perceived bullying against LGBT students as harmless, while 70% of Hanoi parents said they would not allow their children to talk to gay students, some believing conversion therapy could cure LGBT children.

Under legislation enacted in 2006, people infected with HIV and people living with AIDS are protected from discrimination, and health care is provided free to all Vietnamese citizens.

The 2022 conversion-therapy dispatch mandated enhanced public communication across medical facilities nationwide so that staff and patients better understand LGBTQ+ individuals, and advised that psychological support be provided by people with an understanding of gender identity. No law prohibits non-consensual intersex medical interventions.

Public visibility was for a time state-encouraged: the first gay pride parade was held in Hanoi on 5 August 2012, by 2017 events ran in around 34 other cities and provinces with more than 35 held annually in cities including Haiphong, Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City and Cần Thơ, and some events were broadcast on state channels VTV4, VTV6 and VTV9. The Ministry of Labour – Invalids and Social Affairs had earlier, in 2002, declared homosexuality a social evil comparable to prostitution, gambling and drug use and promised legislation to combat homosexuality and arrest same-sex couples.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa and border-document rules for transgender travellers are not covered by any source in this inventory, including whether passport gender markers that differ from presentation trigger additional screening at Vietnamese ports of entry. This is an unresolved gap, not a finding of permissive practice.

Whether the identity-card gender change permitted by the Law on Citizen Identification from 1 July 2024 can in fact be completed without a Gender Affirmation Law in force is not resolved in the sources; the statute's wording ties legal effect to that law's passage, while no source reports a documented case of the change being granted or refused.

Hate-crime provisions covering violence against transgender people are not sourced here. The 2024 United Nations account documents violence risk but does not establish whether aggravated penalties apply.

The availability and cost of gender-affirming care in Vietnam, as distinct from the administrative barriers to legal recognition, are not established by these sources; Outright International records obstacles to care without quantifying them.

Whether the 2025 Pride cancellations were an isolated permit decision or a standing policy is unresolved. Only Ho Chi Minh City and five unnamed 2025 events are identified, and no source reports a 2026 outcome.
